Meeting header
Date/Time: 2026-05-09 16:00 PT
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Sara Patel (Northbridge Platform), Tom Reyes (Northbridge CTO), Eli Huang (SRE), Priya Mistry (Security), Jordan Lee (Product)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
- Intro to Redwood hosted chat generation and streaming behavior.
- Discussed param controls (temperature, max_tokens, top_p), streaming/retry patterns, and quick tradeoffs (latency vs cost).
- Security questions around SOC2, KMS, VPC.
- Agreed next steps: pricing, security docs, and a technical benchmark session.

Topics: streaming behavior, generation params, retries/backoff, latency vs batch cost, security/compliance, integration steps

--- Transcript body ---
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. i'm Maya with Redwood — i'm the AE on this account. quick round of intros?
[00:08] Tom: tom here, CTO at Northbridge. we're building conversational interfaces for customer ops and inventory help.
[00:12] Sara: sara — platform eng, i'll be owning the integration.
[00:16] Eli: eli, sre, i'll watch latency and cost.
[00:19] Priya: priya, security, SOC2 and data residency questions.
[00:22] Jordan: jordan, product — want to see what's possible with streaming responses for live chat.
[00:26] Liam: thanks, i'll be walking through the hosted chat demo and the parameter controls — hi all.

[03:05] Liam: okay so i'm sharing my screen, start with the simple chat endpoint — this is our hosted API. we support both full response generation and streaming. streaming's useful for perceived latency — you get tokens as they arrive. note that we do continuous batching under the hood so small requests get batched conservatively to save cost.
[03:37] Sara: when you say batching, is it time-based? like will you hold a request for 50ms to batch?
[03:44] Liam: good q, it's workload-aware — default target is about 10–30ms tail hold and then you can configure aggressive batching for throughput workloads. for hosted we expose suggestions, for dedicated you get finer controls.
[04:10] Eli: how does that affect p95 latency vs p99?
[04:13] Liam: p95 typically dominated by network and model compute, batching adds a small headroom at p99; we provide dashboards in the console that show token-level latency and batching contribution. sometimes the monitor spells it 'token lat' in the UI.
[05:02] Tom: on retries — if a streaming connection fails mid-response, do you re-try from scratch or can you resume?
[05:08] Liam: short answer: resume isn't supported today for arbitrary KV cache continuation in hosted, so we do retries from the last stable checkpoint. in practice we try to resume from a prefix if the client reports the last received token, but for strict at-most-once you should design idempotency keys and reconcilers.
[05:39] Maya: that's a good point — most customers use the client-side reconstructor to stitch partial streams and we recommend an exponential backoff with jitter for transient 5xx and 429s.

[07:15] Priya: quick security Q — can you describe encryption at rest and KMS integration?
[07:21] Liam: yes. hosted supports customer-managed keys via our KMS integration for dedicated + private tiers; hosted can use platform keys but for data residency or key exclusivity we recommend Dedicated or Private. we also have audit logs and token-level redaction controls.
[07:42] Priya: and SOC2?
[07:44] Maya: we have SOC2 type II and ISO attestation; i'll send the compliance pack after this call.

[09:06] Jordan: product question — curious how params affect hallucination risk. like if i crank temperature down will that make it deterministic?
[09:12] Liam: lowering temperature reduces sampling randomness, so you see less creative outputs and fewer hallucinations on average for factual tasks. also consider using logit bias or retrieval-augmented prompts for grounding. we also have reranking/eval hooks in Optimize to monitor quality regressions over time.
[09:44] Jordan: can Optimize run against streaming outputs?
[09:48] Liam: Optimize currently ingests final generations but you can capture streaming content client-side and submit batches for eval.

[11:05] Sara: demo time — show us a typical request and streaming response.
[11:09] Liam: sure. sample curl: 
POST /v1/chat/generate 
headers: Authorization; Content-Type: application/json
body: { messages: [{ role: user, content: "What's the status of order 12345" }], stream: true, temperature: 0.2, max_tokens: 150 }

[12:20] Liam: in the stream you'll see partial chunks with delta tokens — handle them idempotently, display when you hit the end_of_stream event. note retries: if you get a network disconnect, the client can reconnect and start a fresh request with same conversation history; we recommend passing an idempotency_key to help correlate.
[12:55] Eli: you mentioned rate limits earlier — what does hosted default look like?
[12:59] Maya: hosted starts with soft rate limits per API key, we negotiate higher quotas as usage grows. for big customers we recommend Dedicated to avoid throttling.

[14:40] Tom: cost question — what affects per-token cost? batching, quantization, model family?
[14:45] Liam: exactly — model family is primary (bigger model, higher cost), quantized variants reduce compute cost but may slightly change generation profile. batching reduces cost by amortizing kernel overhead. caching (prefix/KV cache) can make repeated prompts very cheap. we'll produce a cost model that shows tokens, batching savings, and expected monthly spend for your traffic pattern.

[17:02] Sara: do you have any recommended defaults for shopping chat — short responses under 3s?
[17:07] Liam: for sub-3s P95 we suggest low TTF (time-to-first-token) models with streaming enabled, temperature 0–0.3, max_tokens limit of 60, and prioritize routing to lower-latency region. also aggressive prefix caching for repeated prompts helps.

[19:55] Priya: data residency — our legal says certain PII must not leave region. hosted doesn't guarantee region-level residency?
[20:02] Maya: hosted has multiple regions but for strict residency we'd recommend Dedicated with VPC peering or Private deployment (VPC/on-prem). we can run a Private control plane in your cloud for full residency.

[22:30] Tom: if we go Dedicated, can we still get streaming? any functional differences?
[22:35] Liam: streaming is supported in all tiers. Dedicated gives you more tuning knobs — batch windows, autoscale policies, and the ability to pin quantized kernels. Private gives you full control over networking and keys.

[24:10] Jordan: how do rollouts work? we want to canary model changes without affecting prod.
[24:15] Liam: Console supports rollouts — canary percentages, A/B routing, automatic fallback to previous model on error or quality regression. you can tie rollouts to evals in Optimize and have automated rollback if quality drops.

[26:40] Eli: practical note — we already have a rate-limiting gateway in front of our frontends, will Redwood integrate fine?
[26:45] Maya: yes, most customers keep their own gateway. we recommend setting client-side circuit breakers and token-budgeting.

[28:10] Sara: are there client SDKs?
[28:12] Liam: yes — official SDKs for JS, Python, plus a lightweight fetch example. SDKs handle stream parsing, reconnection hints and retry backoffs. sometimes the docs call it the 'conversations' SDK but there are multiple entry points.

[31:00] Tom: curious about telemetry — what traces/metrics do we get?
[31:04] Liam: we expose per-request timing (TTF, tokens generated, batching delay), cost estimates, error types, and traces you can hook into your existing APM. Console shows token breakdown per route and per model.

[33:55] Jordan: demo: show param changes live.
[33:59] Liam: changing temperature live — higher temp makes replies more verbose and sometimes wander. i'm toggling to 0.9 now... you see the output become more exploratory. reduce to 0.1 to be conservative. also max_tokens cap truncates final tokens.

[36:18] Priya: one more security detail — who can see logs? redwood staff?
[36:22] Maya: access to production logs is restricted, and audit logs show any admin access. for enterprise contracts we can provide stricter controls and even log redaction options.

[38:00] Eli: re: retries — do you have built-in retry headers or status codes that differentiate transient vs permanent errors?
[38:07] Liam: yes, we return 5xx for server errors, 429 for rate limits and we try to include a Retry-After header. request ids help correlate and we'll include a partial error code in the stream for easier client logic.

[40:20] Tom: ok, for the benchmark session what do you need from us?
[40:24] Liam: ideally a sample traffic trace (anonymized), target p95 latency and cost goals, and a small prompt set for quality checks. we'll provision a test instance in hosted or dedicated depending on which you prefer.

[42:12] Sara: what about model versions — how do we pin older versions in case of regressions?

[42:16] Liam: Console supports pinning model versions per route, and you can do canary percentage splits. Optimize ties to prompt-based evals so you can detect quality regressions before rolling to 100%.

[44:45] Jordan: any gotchas we should consider for client UI when showing streaming tokens?
[44:49] Liam: show partial token placeholders, apply debounce to avoid janky UI, handle duplicate tokens from reconnects, and always show a finalization marker when end_of_stream arrives. some customers buffer small chunks for UX smoothing.

[46:30] Maya: quick recap — we covered streaming, batching, param effects, retries, security and deployment options.
[46:40] Tom: good — next steps are the pricing sheet and the benchmark deep-dive.

[47:02] Maya: action items: i'll send pricing and SOC2 pack; liam will prep the benchmark plan; tom will confirm windows and share traces.

[49:15] Priya: one last Q — what's your patch for sensitive data in prompts? do you have PII redaction?
[49:21] Liam: we support server-side redaction rules and client-side suggestions. also Configure the retention policy in console for logs and we can enable automatic PII filters for common patterns.

[51:00] Jordan: timeline question — if we like the benchmark, how fast can we go to prod?
[51:05] Maya: for a basic hosted integration it's days to weeks. for Dedicated it's typically a few weeks depending on capacity reservation. Private can be 4–8 weeks based on infra and compliance work.

[52:30] Tom: ok thanks everyone. looking forward to the benchmark.
[52:35] Maya: thanks all, we'll follow up with notes and docs.

End of transcript.
